overview:
Pandit Todarmal (c. 1719–1766 CE) is regarded as one of the most influential lay scholars of the Digambara Jain tradition, especially in the field of Hindi prose, doctrinal commentary, and reformist religious thought. Born in Jaipur to Jogidas Khandelwal and Rambhabai of the Godika gotra, he lived as a householder while embodying a deeply ascetic and contemplative orientation. His life coincided with a period of political instability, sectarian tension, ritual conservatism, and social inequality in eighteenth‑century North India, and his writings consciously address these conditions by returning to what he understood as the core of Jain dharma: right knowledge (samyag‑jñāna), right faith (samyag‑darśana), and right conduct (samyag‑cāritra).

Todarmal’s scholarship is marked by a rare combination of linguistic skill, philosophical depth, and pedagogical clarity. He was well‑versed in Prakrit, Sanskrit, Hindi, and had working knowledge of Kannada, enabling him to read and interpret manuscripts that were inaccessible to many contemporaries. Drawing on extensive study of canonical and post‑canonical Digambara works—such as Samayasāra, Pañcāstikāya, Pravacanasāra, Niyamasāra, Gommatasāra (Jīvakāṇḍa and Karmakāṇḍa), Labdhisāra, Trilokasāra, Kṣapaṇāsāra, Purūṣārthasiddhyupāya, and others—he produced Hindi commentaries and independent treatises that sought to make subtle doctrinal points intelligible to lay audiences without sacrificing rigor.

His most celebrated independent work, "Mokṣa‑mārga‑prakāśaka" (Illuminator of the Path to Liberation), systematizes the Jain path in accessible Hindi, emphasizing the distinction between the pure self (śuddha‑jīva) and karmic bondage, and warning against ritualism devoid of right understanding. Alongside this, his commentarial corpus—often described as running to tens of thousands of verses and several thousand pages—includes detailed Hindi expositions on Gommatasāra (Jīvakāṇḍa and Karmakāṇḍa), Labdhisāra, Kṣapaṇāsāra, and Trilokasāra, among others. These works not only clarify technical doctrines of karma, cosmology, and spiritual progression but also attempt to harmonize apparent tensions between texts that focus on the pure soul and those that analyze empirical, karmic states.

Todarmal is also remembered as a reformer within the Digambara community. He played a leading role in shaping the Digambara Terāpanthī style of practice in Jaipur, which was critical of the then‑dominant bhattāraka institution and of tantric and magical ritualism. His emphasis on scriptural study, ethical discipline, and simplicity of worship contributed to the emergence of a Terāpanthī community that prioritized doctrinal clarity over elaborate external observances. After his death, his son Gumanirām further radicalized this trajectory, giving rise to the Guman‑panth or "śuddha Terāpanth" (pure Terāpanth), which tightened rules of conduct and ritual purity.

Historically, Todarmal’s influence extended beyond Jaipur. Contemporary and later testimonies describe him as a sought‑after theological authority whose presence drew large audiences to religious assemblies. Diwans and other officials of Jaipur reportedly attended his discourses, and letters from fellow scholars praise his ability to resolve complex doctrinal doubts. At the same time, his reformist stance and critique of entrenched interests made him a controversial figure. Some traditional accounts narrate that he was falsely accused of desecrating a Śiva liṅga and executed under political pressure, underscoring the risks faced by religious reformers in his milieu.

From the perspective of Jain intellectual history, Todarmal stands at a crucial junction: he bridges classical Digambara scholasticism and early modern vernacular religious literature. His mixed Hindi style—drawing on Braj, Dhundhārī (Jaipuri), and Khari Boli—helped make complex doctrinal material accessible to lay readers and is of interest to scholars studying the evolution of North Indian prose. Within Jain studies, his works remain important for understanding how eighteenth‑century Digambara thinkers received, systematized, and transmitted earlier doctrinal traditions, especially in relation to karma theory, cosmology, and the path to liberation.

Modern scholarship, including detailed studies by Dr. Hukamchand Bharilla and others, has attempted to reconstruct Todarmal’s biography and corpus from scattered manuscript evidence and community memory. While exact dates and circumstances of his life are not always uniformly reported, a broad consensus places his birth around 1719–1720 CE and his death around 1766–1767 CE, with a relatively short but extraordinarily productive lifespan of about forty‑seven years. His legacy continues in the ongoing study of his commentaries, the institutional memory of Terāpanthī and Guman‑panth communities, and the wider appreciation of his role as a lay scholar who combined rigorous textual engagement with a reformist, ethically focused vision of Jain practice.

primary_sources.title: Mokṣa‑mārga‑prakāśaka
primary_sources.author: Pandit Todarmal
primary_sources.translation: The path to liberation is characterized by the union of right knowledge, right faith, and right conduct.
primary_sources.notes: This formulation reflects the central doctrinal emphasis of Todarmal’s "Mokṣa‑mārga‑prakāśaka": liberation (mokṣa) depends on the integrated cultivation of samyag‑jñāna, samyag‑darśana, and samyag‑cāritra. The work is composed in mixed Hindi with frequent Sanskrit and Prakrit technical terms, and serves as a systematic guide for lay practitioners. Exact wording may vary slightly across manuscripts and printed editions; the line here represents a doctrinally faithful formulation rather than a critical edition reading.

primary_sources.title: Gommatasāra Jīvakāṇḍa (Hindi commentary)
primary_sources.author: Pandit Todarmal (commentator); original text by Ācārya Nemicandra
primary_sources.translation: The soul becomes of many kinds, according to its states of bondage and liberation.
primary_sources.notes: Todarmal’s Hindi commentary on Gommatasāra Jīvakāṇḍa explains technical classifications of souls (jīva) in relation to karmic bondage, spiritual development, and liberation. His glosses aim to clarify dense Prakrit verses for lay readers, often paraphrasing and expanding on Nemicandra’s original. The cited line is representative of the text’s focus on differentiating souls by their karmic condition; precise verse numbering and wording should be checked against a critical edition.

primary_sources.title: Gommatasāra Karmakāṇḍa (Hindi commentary)
primary_sources.author: Pandit Todarmal (commentator); original text by Ācārya Nemicandra
primary_sources.original_text: karmaṇāṃ prakṛtayaḥ puṇyāpuṇyāś ca jīvānāṃ bandha‑hetavaḥ
primary_sources.transliteration: karmaṇāṃ prakṛtayaḥ puṇyā‑apuṇyāś ca jīvānāṃ bandha‑hetavaḥ
primary_sources.translation: The natures of karmas, meritorious and demeritorious, are causes of the bondage of souls.
primary_sources.notes: In his commentary on Gommatasāra Karmakāṇḍa, Todarmal elaborates the taxonomy of karmas, their qualities (prakṛti), and their role in binding the soul. He frequently connects these technical discussions to practical ethical concerns, warning against both gross sins and subtle attachment. The line given summarizes a core doctrinal point; as with other citations, exact phrasing may differ among manuscripts, and should be verified in scholarly editions.

primary_sources.title: Labdhisāra (Hindi commentary)
primary_sources.author: Pandit Todarmal (commentator); original text traditionally attributed to Ācārya Nemicandra
primary_sources.translation: Attainment (labdhi) is the acquisition of right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct.
primary_sources.notes: Todarmal’s Hindi exposition of Labdhisāra discusses stages of spiritual attainment and the conditions under which right faith, knowledge, and conduct arise and stabilize. He uses accessible examples and vernacular language to explain technical categories, making the text a bridge between scholastic doctrine and lay practice. The line encapsulates the central theme of labdhi as spiritual acquisition; textual details should be confirmed against reliable editions.

primary_sources.title: Kṣapaṇāsāra (Hindi commentary)
primary_sources.author: Pandit Todarmal (commentator); original text traditionally attributed to Ācārya Nemicandra
primary_sources.translation: Kṣapaṇā is the shedding (nirjarā) of sins.
primary_sources.notes: In his commentary on Kṣapaṇāsāra, Todarmal focuses on the processes by which karmic particles, especially those associated with sinful actions, are exhausted and shed. He links doctrinal descriptions of nirjarā to concrete practices of restraint, confession, and inner transformation. The cited definition reflects a standard Jain understanding of kṣapaṇā; as with other examples, it should be treated as representative rather than as a critical‑edition quotation.

misconceptions.myth: Todarmal was the same person as Raja Todar Mal, the Mughal finance minister of Emperor Akbar.
misconceptions.reality: Pandit Todarmal was an eighteenth‑century Digambara Jain lay scholar based primarily in Jaipur, active in religious reform and doctrinal commentary. Raja Todar Mal, by contrast, was a sixteenth‑century Mughal official and courtier. They lived in different centuries, in different roles, and belong to distinct historical and religious contexts.

misconceptions.myth: Todarmal was a fully ordained Jain monk and head of a traditional monastic lineage.
misconceptions.reality: Available historical and community sources consistently describe Todarmal as a householder (śrāvaka) who lived a highly ascetic and scholarly life but did not function as a formal monk (muni) or bhattāraka. His authority derived from scriptural mastery, ethical conduct, and reformist leadership within lay communities, not from holding a monastic office.

misconceptions.myth: Todarmal founded the Śvetāmbara Terāpanth sect and is directly linked to later Terāpanthī monastic lineages.
misconceptions.reality: Todarmal’s reform work took place within the Digambara tradition and is associated with the Digambara Terāpanthī style of practice in Jaipur. The Śvetāmbara Terāpanth, with its own distinct history and leadership, emerged later in a different regional and sectarian context. While the term "Terāpanth" appears in multiple Jain traditions, these groups should not be conflated.

misconceptions.myth: There is complete certainty and uniform agreement about every detail of Todarmal’s biography, including his exact birth and death dates and the circumstances of his death.
misconceptions.reality: Modern research, especially by scholars such as Dr. Hukamchand Bharilla, has reconstructed Todarmal’s life from manuscripts, inscriptions, and community memory, yielding widely accepted approximate dates (c. 1719–1720 CE for birth and c. 1766–1767 CE for death). However, some details—such as the precise circumstances of his death and the exact chronology of certain works—remain subject to debate and rely on circumstantial evidence rather than definitive documentation.

misconceptions.myth: Todarmal’s writings are purely ritual manuals with little philosophical content.
misconceptions.reality: Although Todarmal did compose some works related to ritual (such as Gommatasāra‑pūjā and other liturgical texts), the core of his corpus consists of philosophically rich commentaries and independent treatises that address karma theory, cosmology, the nature of the soul, and the path to liberation. His reputation in Jain intellectual history rests precisely on his ability to clarify complex doctrinal material for lay audiences while maintaining philosophical depth.
